ja: だいななじゅうはちかい

p.src: Now the King of Hanzhong, on hearing that Lord Guan and his son had been slain, wept until he collapsed to the ground; the civil and military officers hurried to revive him, and only after a long while did he regain consciousness and was helped into the inner hall. Kongming consoled him, saying, “My lord, temper your grief. As the ancient saying goes, ‘Life and death are ordained by fate.’ Lord Guan was always unyielding and proud, and that is why this calamity befell him today. For now, Your Highness should preserve your noble health and slowly plan how to avenge him.” Xuande said, “When I swore brotherhood with my two younger brothers Guan and Zhang in the Peach Garden, we vowed to share life and death. Now that Yunchang is dead, how can I enjoy wealth and honor alone?” Before he had finished speaking, Guan Xing came in, wailing bitterly. At the sight of him, Xuande gave a great cry and again wept himself unconscious upon the ground. The officers revived him. Each day he fainted from weeping three or five times; for three days he took neither water nor broth, but only wept in anguish; his tears soaked his robe, leaving it mottled with blood. Kongming and the officers repeatedly sought to comfort him. Xuande said, “I swear that Eastern Wu and I shall not endure together beneath the sun and moon!” Kongming said, “I hear that Eastern Wu presented Lord Guan’s head to Cao Cao, and Cao Cao buried him with the rites due to a prince and noble.” Xuande asked, “What is the meaning of this?” Kongming replied, “Eastern Wu meant to shift the blame onto Cao Cao. Cao Cao saw through their scheme and therefore buried Lord Guan with lavish honors, so that Your Highness would direct your resentment against Wu.” Xuande said, “I shall raise an army this very moment and call Wu to account, that I may wash away my hatred!” Kongming remonstrated, “You must not. At present Wu wishes us to attack Wei, while Wei wishes us to attack Wu. Each harbors a treacherous design and waits to exploit an opening. Your Highness should keep the army still and first hold the funeral rites for Lord Guan. When Wu and Wei fall out, we may seize the moment to attack. That would be best.” The officers also remonstrated with him again and again. Only then did Xuande take food, and he issued an order that every officer and soldier throughout the Riverlands should put on mourning. The King of Hanzhong went in person beyond the southern gate to summon the soul and perform the funeral sacrifices, wailing the entire day.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao was in Luoyang. Ever since he buried Lord Guan, whenever he closed his eyes at night he would see him. Cao Cao was greatly frightened and asked his officers about it. The officers said, “The old halls of the temporary palace at Luoyang are much haunted. You should build a new hall and reside there.” Cao Cao said, “I wish to erect a hall and name it the Jianshi Hall. I regret only that I have no skilled craftsman.” Jia Xu said, “There is a skilled craftsman in Luoyang named Su Yue, whose ingenuity is unsurpassed.” Cao Cao summoned him and ordered him to draw up a design. Su Yue drew a great nine-bay hall, with galleries, side chambers, towers, and pavilions before and behind, and presented the design to Cao Cao. Cao Cao examined it and said, “Your design accords perfectly with my wishes, but I fear we lack timber fit for the ridge beam and pillars.” Su Yue said, “Thirty li from the city lies a pool called the Leaping Dragon Pool. Before it stands a shrine called the Leaping Dragon Shrine. Beside the shrine grows a great pear tree more than ten zhang tall, which would serve as a beam for the Jianshi Hall.”

p.src: Cao Cao was delighted and immediately sent workmen there to fell it. The next day they returned to report that no saw could cut the tree and no axe could bite into it, so they had been unable to fell it. Cao Cao did not believe them. He personally led several hundred horsemen straight to the Leaping Dragon Shrine, dismounted before it, and looked up at the tree. It rose tall and stately like a splendid canopy, pierced the clouds, and had not a single crooked knot. Cao Cao ordered it cut down, but several village elders came forward and remonstrated, “This tree is already several hundred years old, and a divine being often dwells upon it. We fear it must not be felled.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and said, “For more than forty years I have traveled throughout the realm beneath heaven. From the Son of Heaven above to the common people below, none fails to fear me; what demon or spirit is this that dares oppose my will?” With that, he drew the sword at his side and struck the tree himself. It rang out with a metallic clang, and blood spattered all over him. Cao Cao was stunned and terrified. He threw down his sword, mounted his horse, and returned to the palace. That night, during the second watch, Cao Cao could not rest in his bed. He sat in the hall, leaned against an armrest, and dozed off. Suddenly he saw a man with loose hair, bearing a sword and dressed in black, stride directly before him. Pointing at Cao Cao, the man shouted, “I am the spirit of the pear tree. You intend to build the Jianshi Hall as part of your design to usurp the throne, and now you come to fell my sacred tree! I know that the number of your days is exhausted, and I have come expressly to kill you!” Cao Cao was horrified and hastily cried, “Where are my guards?” The man in black raised his sword to strike Cao Cao. Cao Cao gave a great cry and suddenly awoke in terror, his head aching beyond endurance; he urgently issued an order to seek skilled physicians everywhere; but none of their treatments could cure him. All the officers were anxious.

p.src: Hua Xin entered and memorialized, “Does Your Highness know of the divine physician Hua Tuo?” Cao Cao said, “Do you mean the man who treated Zhou Tai in Jiangdong?” Hua Xin said, “The very man.” Cao Cao said, “Though I have heard his name, I do not know the nature of his art.” Hua Xin said, “Hua Tuo, whose courtesy name is Yuanhua, is a native of Qiao Commandery in the state of Pei. His marvelous skill in medicine is rarely equaled in the world. Whenever anyone is ill, whether he uses medicine, needles, or moxibustion, the patient is cured as readily as his hand moves. If a disease of the internal organs cannot be helped by medicine, he gives the patient Ma Fei Decoction to drink, rendering him as insensible as if drunk or dead. He then cuts open the abdomen with a sharp knife and washes the organs with a medicinal solution, while the patient feels not the slightest pain. When the washing is complete, he stitches the opening with medicated thread and applies medicine to it; after a month, or perhaps only twenty days, the patient is fully restored. Such are his divine powers. One day, while Hua Tuo was traveling along a road, he heard a man groaning. Hua Tuo said, ‘This is an illness that prevents food and drink from passing down.’ He questioned the man and found it was indeed so. Hua Tuo had him drink three sheng of garlic-and-pickle juice. The man vomited up a snake two or three chi long, and at once could swallow food again. Chen Deng, Governor of Guangling, suffered distress in his chest, a flushed face, and an inability to eat or drink, so he sought treatment from Hua Tuo. Hua Tuo gave him medicine to drink, whereupon he vomited three sheng of worms, all red-headed and writhing from head to tail. Chen Deng asked the cause. Hua Tuo said, ‘This poison arose because you ate too much raw fish. Though you are cured today, it will certainly return three years hence, and then you cannot be saved.’ Indeed, Chen Deng died three years later. There was also a man who developed a tumor between his eyebrows that itched unbearably, and he asked Hua Tuo to examine it. Hua Tuo said, ‘There is a flying creature inside it.’ Everyone laughed at him. Hua Tuo cut it open with a knife, and a yellow sparrow flew out; the patient was cured at once. Another man was bitten on the toe by a dog, after which two lumps of flesh grew there. One hurt and the other itched, both beyond endurance. Hua Tuo said, ‘Inside the painful one are ten needles, and inside the itching one are two black-and-white gaming stones.’ No one believed him. Hua Tuo cut them open with a knife, and everything proved exactly as he had said. This man is truly of the same order as Bian Que and Cang Gong. He now resides in Jincheng, not far from here. Why does Your Highness not summon him?”

p.src: Cao Cao immediately sent men to bring Hua Tuo with all speed, day and night. Once admitted, he was ordered to take Cao Cao’s pulse and examine his illness. Hua Tuo said, “Your Highness’s headache arose from an affliction of wind. The root of the illness lies within the skull, where the wind-borne fluid cannot escape. It is useless to take medicinal decoctions; they cannot cure it. I have one method: first drink Ma Fei Decoction, then have the skull split open with a sharp axe and the wind-borne fluid removed. Only then can the root of the illness be eradicated.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and said, “Do you mean to kill me?” Hua Tuo said, “Your Highness must have heard that when Lord Guan was struck by a poisoned arrow and wounded in his right arm, I scraped the bone to remove the poison, and Lord Guan showed not the slightest fear. Why then is Your Highness so suspicious over so slight an ailment?” Cao Cao said, “An aching arm may be scraped, but how can a skull be split open? You must have been close to Lord Guan and intend to seize this opportunity to avenge him!” He called to his attendants to seize Hua Tuo, cast him into prison, and interrogate him under torture about his intent. Jia Xu remonstrated, “A skilled physician such as this has scarcely an equal in the world. We must not cast him away.” Cao Cao rebuked him, saying, “This man means to seize the opportunity to harm me. He is no different from Ji Ping!” He urgently ordered that Hua Tuo be subjected to further interrogation under torture.

p.src: While Hua Tuo was in prison, there was a jailer surnamed Wu, whom everyone called Jailer Wu. Every day, this man brought Hua Tuo wine and food. Grateful for his kindness, Hua Tuo told him, “I shall soon die, and my one regret is that my Book of the Green Satchel has not been handed down to the world. I am deeply moved by your kindness, yet have no other means of repaying you. I will write a letter; send someone with it to my home to fetch the Book of the Green Satchel, and I shall give it to you so that you may carry on my art.” Jailer Wu was overjoyed. “If I obtain that book, I shall resign this post and heal the sick throughout the realm, thereby perpetuating your virtue.” Hua Tuo at once wrote the letter and gave it to Jailer Wu. Jailer Wu went straight to Jincheng, obtained the Book of the Green Satchel from Hua Tuo’s wife, then returned to the prison and handed it to Hua Tuo. After examining it, Hua Tuo gave the book to Jailer Wu. Jailer Wu took it home and hid it away. Ten days later, Hua Tuo died in prison. Jailer Wu bought a coffin and completed the funeral rites; then, having resigned his post, he returned home intending to study the Book of the Green Satchel, only to find his wife burning it. Jailer Wu was aghast and hastened to snatch it away, but the entire volume had already burned, leaving only a page or two. In fury, Jailer Wu berated his wife. His wife said, “Even if you mastered arts as wondrous as Hua Tuo’s, you would only end by dying in prison. What use would they be?” Jailer Wu could only sigh and desist. Thus the Book of the Green Satchel was never transmitted to the world. All that survived were minor methods such as castrating chickens and pigs, recorded on the one or two leaves spared by the fire. A later poet lamented in verse:

As he pondered anxiously, a close attendant suddenly reported that Eastern Wu had sent an envoy bearing a memorial.
Cao Cao took the letter, opened it, and read.
In substance, it said:

p.src: When Cao Cao had finished reading, he laughed heartily, showed the letter to his ministers, and said, “Does this fellow mean to set me atop a blazing furnace?” Chen Qun, the Palace Attendant, and others memorialized, “The House of Han has long been in decline. Your Highness’s achievements and virtue tower above all, and the people look to you with hope. Now Sun Quan has declared himself your subject and submitted to your command. This is the accord of Heaven and humankind, with portents and voices alike proclaiming it. Your Highness should answer Heaven and follow the people by promptly ascending the imperial throne.” Cao Cao laughed. “I have served Han for many years. Though my achievements and virtue have benefited the people, I have risen to the rank of king, the utmost limit of title and honor. How could I dare aspire to anything more? If the Mandate of Heaven truly rests with me, then I shall be King Wen of Zhou.” Sima Yi said, “Since Sun Quan has declared himself your subject and submitted, Your Majesty may confer office and rank upon him and order him to resist Liu Bei.” Cao Cao followed his counsel and submitted a memorial appointing Sun Quan General of Agile Cavalry, Marquis of Nanchang, and Governor of Jingzhou. That same day, an envoy was dispatched to Eastern Wu bearing the imperial patent and decree.

p.src: Cao Cao’s illness worsened further. One night he suddenly dreamed of three horses feeding from the same trough. At dawn he asked Jia Xu, “Some time ago, I dreamed of three horses at one trough and suspected that Ma Teng and his sons would bring disaster. Ma Teng is now dead, yet last night I again dreamed of three horses feeding from one trough. Does it portend good or ill?” Jia Xu replied, “The emolument-horse is an auspicious omen. The emolument-horses are returning to Cao; why need Your Majesty harbor any doubts?” Thereafter Cao Cao dismissed his doubts. A later poet wrote:

p.src: That night Cao Cao lay in his bedchamber. At the third watch, feeling dizzy and his vision swimming, he rose and lay with his head upon a writing table. Suddenly he heard a sound in the hall like silk being torn. Looking up in alarm, he saw Empress Fu, Lady Dong, the two imperial princes, Fu Wan, Dong Cheng, and more than twenty others, their bodies drenched in blood, standing amid clouds of sorrow; faintly he heard them demanding his life. Cao Cao hastily drew his sword and slashed at the empty air. Suddenly a tremendous crash shook down the southwestern corner of the palace. Cao Cao fell senseless in terror. His attendants rescued him and moved him to another palace to recuperate. The following night, the unceasing cries of men and women were again heard outside the palace. At dawn Cao Cao summoned his ministers and said, “For more than thirty years amid war and cavalry, I have never believed in strange or supernatural matters. Why, then, has this happened to me today?” The ministers memorialized, “Your Majesty should order Daoist priests to perform a sacrificial rite and conduct ceremonies to avert calamity.” Cao Cao sighed. “The Sage said, ‘One who has offended against Heaven has nowhere to pray.’ My allotted span under Heaven is exhausted. How could I be saved?” He therefore refused to permit the rite.

p.src: The next day he felt his vital breath surge into his upper chest and lost his sight, so he urgently summoned Xiahou Dun for counsel. When Xiahou Dun reached the palace gate, he suddenly saw Empress Fu, Lady Dong, the two imperial princes, Fu Wan, Dong Cheng, and the others standing amid dark clouds. Xiahou Dun was so terrified that he fainted. His attendants carried him away, and from that time onward he fell ill. Cao Cao summoned Cao Hong, Chen Qun, Jia Xu, Sima Yi, and the others to his bedside and entrusted them with his final affairs. Cao Hong and the others bowed their heads to the floor and said, “May Your Majesty take good care of your precious person. Before many days have passed, you will surely recover completely.” Cao Cao said, “For more than thirty years I have swept unhindered across the realm, and all the rival lords have been destroyed. u.src: The next day he felt his vital breath surge into his upper chest and lost his sight, so he urgently summoned Xiahou Dun for counsel.
When Xiahou Dun reached the palace gate, he suddenly saw Empress Fu, Lady Dong, the two imperial princes, Fu Wan, Dong Cheng, and the others standing amid dark clouds.
Xiahou Dun was so terrified that he fainted. His attendants carried him away, and from that time onward he fell ill.
Cao Cao summoned Cao Hong, Chen Qun, Jia Xu, Sima Yi, and the others to his bedside and entrusted them with his final affairs.
Cao Hong and the others bowed their heads to the floor and said, “May Your Majesty take good care of your precious person. Before many days have passed, you will surely recover completely.”

p.src: Cao Hong and the others accepted the command in tears and withdrew. Cao Cao ordered his attendants to bring out the fine incense he had long kept and divided it among his concubines. He instructed them, “After my death, you must diligently practice women’s handiwork and make many silk slippers, which you may sell to earn money for your own support.” He further ordered that his concubines should mostly reside in the Bronze Bird Terrace, where sacrifices were to be offered daily, with female musicians required to perform and present food. He also left orders that seventy-two false tombs be established outside Jiangwu City in Zhangde Prefecture, so that later generations would not know where he was buried, for fear that men might dig up his grave. p.src: Now when Cao Cao died, all the civil and military officials went into mourning; at the same time, messengers were sent to announce the death to the heir Cao Pi, Cao Zhang, Marquis of Yanling, Cao Zhi, Marquis of Linzi, and Cao Xiong, Marquis Huai of Xiao. The officials laid Cao Cao in a golden coffin within a silver outer casket, then bore his bier through the night toward Ye Commandery. When Cao Pi learned of his father's death, he burst into bitter weeping and led officials high and low ten li beyond the city, where they prostrated themselves by the road to receive the bier; they escorted it into the city and placed it in a side hall. The officials donned mourning dress and gathered in the hall to weep. Suddenly one man stepped forward and said, “I beg Your Highness to restrain your grief and first deliberate upon the affairs of state.” They looked and saw that it was Sima Fu, Palace Attendant to the Heir Apparent. Sima Fu said, “Now that the King of Wei has passed away, the whole realm is shaken. A successor king must be installed without delay to settle the hearts of the people. Why do nothing but weep?” The ministers said, “The heir should indeed succeed to the throne, but we have not yet received an imperial edict. How can we act so hastily?” Chen Jiao, Minister of War, said, “The king died away from the capital. If his beloved sons establish themselves privately and trouble arises between them, the state itself will be imperiled.” He drew his sword, sliced off his own sleeve, and cried sternly, “This very day, I call upon the heir to succeed to the throne. If any official objects, let this sleeve show what shall be done to him!” All the officials trembled in fear. Suddenly it was reported that Hua Xin had arrived at full gallop from Xuchang. Everyone was greatly startled. Presently Hua Xin entered. They asked why he had come. Hua Xin said, “Now that the King of Wei has passed away and the whole realm is shaken, why have you not promptly asked the heir to succeed to the throne?” The officials said, “Precisely because there is no time to await an imperial edict, we were discussing whether to establish the heir as king by a gracious decree from Lady Bian, the queen dowager.” Hua Xin said, “I have already obtained an imperial edict from the Emperor of Han. Here it is.” They all leapt for joy and offered their congratulations. Hua Xin drew the edict from within his robe, opened it, and read it aloud. In truth, Hua Xin was currying favor with Wei; he had therefore drafted this edict himself and coerced Emperor Xian into granting it. The emperor had no choice but to comply, and thus issued an edict appointing Cao Pi King of Wei, Chancellor, and Governor of Ji Province. That very day Cao Pi ascended the throne and received the obeisance and salutations of officials high and low.
